This paper introduces the time-varying Poisson model, a recent econometric approach designed to capture dynamic relationships within count time series data. Additionally, the selected time-varying elements align with known dynamics in the data, and the regularizing parameter adapts to the series length without needing manual adjustment. Furthermore, we extend this framework to a multivariate setting and provide an application demonstrating the model's ability to account for spillover effects between count time series. These investigations will become feasible with upcoming sensitive multi-wavelength facilities, including the Atacames Astronomicos Intercontinentales (IAU), the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), and the Advanced LIGO and Virgo detectors. To maximize the utility of existing multi-wavelength datasets, we have made the data and analysis code for this study publicly accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/AndresBrito/BHDistribution.

The results indicate that the position expectation value linearly follows the direction of the driving force, while the wavefunction widens under time-dependent driving but remains unchanged under constant forcing. These findings align with the system's known physical properties; specifically, the linear response of the position expectation value to the driving force under constant forcing reflects the Heisenberg equation of motion for the harmonic oscillator, and the lack of wavefunction spreading stems from the uniform potential experienced by the particle across different positions. Under constant forcing, the ground state simply shifts along the direction of the force, whereas under time-dependent driving, the particle exhibits behavior analogous to being acted upon by a bat, consistent with soccer free kicks or baseball hits. Under such conditions, the particle behaves like a simple harmonic oscillator, generating Larmor-like precession in its spin under the influence of the driving force. Although this scenario resembles a simple harmonic oscillator, the underlying mechanism is the constant potential difference under time-dependent driving, which creates a uniform potential gradient similar to that caused by a constant driving force. Consequently, the particle responds as if subjected to a constant effective force. Under these circumstances, the simulation under time-dependent driving yields identical outcomes to those under constant effective forcing, aside from the specific nature of the driving force itself. These experiments under time-dependent driving serve primarily to validate the simulation's correctness, as the systems are physically equivalent. To explore more complex dynamics, we considered an asymmetric double-well potential, where the particle can exist in either well, forming a superposition state. In these simulations with sudden potential well changes, the effective potential becomes time-dependent, mimicking the effect of a constant effective force. We introduce a variant of the quantum relational Hoare logic from Unruh (POPL 2019) that incorporates "expectations" into pre- and postconditions. This approach enables reasoning about program performance with relationally specified bounds, ensuring that quantum algorithms adhere to desired bounds on violation probabilities and success probabilities. Furthermore, it facilitates relationally composed reasoning regarding these performance bounds. To support this, we define a theory of bounded expectations and develop a set of expectation-based inference rules. These rules allow for reasoning about bounded terms and bounded implications, and they guarantee that bounded expectations satisfy linearity and Frobenius properties. Soundness is verified through a semantic model comprising bounded terms and terms defined over a specific range of expectations. Our soundness proof utilizes a "relaxation" technique, which involves reasoning about unbounded expectations before ultimately restricting them to the intended range. The theoretical soundness has been corroborated by an automated proof within Isabelle/HOL. Additionally, practical utility is demonstrated through applications to quantum bounded term calculi and quantum relational Hoare logic, as detailed in the full version of this work.

This study examines the bias inherent in the line-of-sight perpendicular component ($B_{\perp}$) of vector magnetic field maps, a metric used to assess the isotropy of these fields. While previous research primarily focused on $B_{\perp}$ measurement errors caused by noise and the inversion algorithm's non-linearity near singularities, this work investigates additional sources of bias. Specifically, we analyze the impact of limited spatial coverage in the observed magnetic network and the limitations of the Global Carbon Model (GCM) boundary conditions. Through Monte Carlo simulations, we quantify these effects and propose a correction method for the $B_{\perp}$ data derived from Phoenix/GONG outputs. The corrected measurements are then integrated into an MHD model (ifMare) to evaluate their influence on predicted magnetic field line connectivity and the perpendicular component's overall isotropy. The findings indicate that both the GCM boundary constraints and the spatial coverage of the monitored network significantly contribute to measurement bias, with coverage being the more dominant factor. Ultimately, the study underscores the necessity for a comprehensive global network of magnetometers to ensure accurate determination of the perpendicular component's isotropy. Additionally, the research suggests that minor inaccuracies in $B_{\perp}$ data are unlikely to substantially alter MHD models' predictions regarding plasma flow velocities. As a practical guideline, this work offers a simple test to identify regions in vector magnetic field maps where $B_{\perp}$ exceeds 100 G, flagging areas that warrant further scrutiny. Ultimately, the insights gained here are applicable to all MHD models utilizing boundary conditions derived from observed magnetic fields.

Among the most critical hyperparameters for neural networks, the loss function plays a pivotal role, yet selecting the appropriate one remains challenging due to the vast array of available options. Although cross entropy is the most widely adopted loss for supervised classification tasks, this study argues that other functions, such as the weighted amended mean absolute error (WAEMAE), can yield superior results. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that adopting WAEMAE instead of cross entropy can significantly enhance performance across a wide range of datasets, often rivaling deep architectures like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTMs). These findings suggest that optimizing the loss function is a more effective strategy than upgrading the underlying network architecture. To validate these conclusions, we conducted comprehensive evaluations on over 200 diverse datasets, including those with multi-label, sequential, and sparse characteristics, utilizing a simple D-NeXt model. Furthermore, we analyzed the training dynamics to understand how different loss functions influence optimization, supported by theoretical insights into the suitability of WAEMAE for supervised classification. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/robertberger/DNeXtLoss.

Cardiac auscultation serves as a vital non-invasive technique for the early detection of heart conditions, yet automatic analysis remains challenging due to the complexity of heart sound signals and the scarcity of public datasets. This study proposes a hybrid framework for the automatic classification of heart sounds, designed to address the limitations of single-based classification methods. The proposed hybrid approach integrates time-frequency domain techniques with time-series-based techniques. Specifically, the time-frequency component utilizes a U-Net architecture for feature extraction, while the time-series component employs either Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) or Convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM) networks. The framework was evaluated using the open-access PhysioNet/CinC 2016 Heart Sound dataset, yielding an accurate classification of four distinct heart sound categories. The results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid model outperforms both traditional time-frequency methods and conventional single-based classification strategies on the PhysioNet/CinC 2016 dataset, achieving an F1-score of 89.09%, precision of 88.81%, recall of 89.37%, and a mean average precision (MAP) of 88.01%. These findings indicate that the hybrid model effectively overcomes the challenges associated with classifying heart sound data, offering significant potential for early heart disease diagnosis through cardiac auscultation. Consequently, this approach could reduce healthcare costs and mitigate the global burden of heart disease. Future work will focus on expanding the dataset to include a broader range of heart sound classifications and further refining the model's performance.

We demonstrate that for ASEP with step initial conditions and a second-class particle originating at zero, the particle's expected velocity converges to a specific speed $s$ as time approaches infinity, provided the parameter $\alpha$ is strictly between 0 and $s$. This result affirmatively settles Conjecture 4.2 from [CGS20]. Additionally, we prove that the probability of the second-class particle maintaining its expected velocity equal to its instantaneous speed throughout evolution vanishes as time goes to infinity. These findings indicate that, unlike in TASEP and classical ASEP, the second-class particle in ASEP exhibits non-trivial behavioral changes over time. The analysis relies on the explicit product-form stationary measure for a multi-shock configuration recently detailed in [BCL20], combined with techniques from [BCLG20] to establish the constant speed of this configuration. Ultimately, the dynamical behavior of the second-class particle emerges as a consequence of the evolution of the surrounding multi-shock setup.

It remains uncertain if bulge expansion causes the flattening of the star-forming main sequence (MS) at high masses. To examine how bulges influence the MS, we analyzed the NUV$-r$ color—a reliable tracer of specific star formation rate—in the central ($r<R_{50}$) versus outer regions of 6,447 local star-forming galaxies. Our results show that for galaxies with $M_{\ast}<10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, the central NUV$-r$ is only about 0.25 magnitudes redder than the outer regions. However, above $M_{\ast}=10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, the central NUV$-r$ becomes significantly redder than the outer regions, indicating that bulges in massive galaxies are more evolved. When sorting galaxies by S\'ersic index $n$, those with $n$>2.0 exhibit redder central NUV$-r$ colors than those with $n$<2.0, even when controlling for B/T ratio and $M_{\ast}$. This implies that bulge star formation depends more strongly on $n$ (or central mass density) than on the B/T ratio. Furthermore, the fraction of galaxies with $n$>2.0 rises sharply with mass for $M_{\ast}>10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, aligning with the turnover in the MS at this transition mass. We conclude that the growing proportion of low specific star formation rate bulges in galaxies with $M_{\ast}>10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, rather than an increase in B/T, drives the flattening of the $M_{\ast}$$-$SFR relation at high masses. This supports the idea that the MS and fundamental planes are interconnected. Additionally, our data support the hypothesis that the transition from spin-dominated to orbit-dominated bulge formation occurs near $M_{\ast}=10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. To further explore this, we prepared the central $R_{50}$-$M_{\ast}$ and (central SFR)$^{\rm on}$-$M_{\ast}$ relations for future simulations investigating baryonic feedback and the transition in bulge formation mechanisms.

Fake news spreads rapidly on social media, endangering public safety and undermining trust in media institutions. While deep learning models perform well on labeled data, their efficacy often drops when encountering fake news related to events they were not trained on. To address this, existing solutions typically rely on integrating data from new events into models before detection, yet this is often impractical. Furthermore, unsupervised methods have been proposed to detect fake news on emergent events without needing new training data; however, these approaches usually depend on extracting features from an entire dataset of potential fake news. This requirement becomes problematic when only a limited number of identified fake news items are available. In this study, we introduce a method to detect fake news on emerging events using a small dataset, leveraging graph neural networks and an unsupervised strategy that requires no training data. Specifically, we utilize an embedding technique for a small-scale fake news dataset combined with graph convolutional networks. Our approach involves three steps: first, an embedding method is applied to the small fake news dataset; second, a shared weight matrix derived from the features of a large dataset (used during the initial phase) is transferred to the small dataset's embeddings; finally, a graph convolutional network is employed for detection on the small dataset. Extensive experiments conducted across multiple datasets demonstrate that our method achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art solutions. Additionally, the feasibility of this strategy was successfully validated on a real-time fake news dataset.

Laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) represents a minimally invasive approach for ablating intracranial structures to manage recurrent intracranial meningiomas (IM). This study aimed to evaluate the clinical outcomes of LITT through a large-scale, single-institution analysis. The methodology involved a retrospective review of 20 consecutive IM patients who underwent LITT between September 2015 and September 2019 at a single center. All procedures were performed under general anesthesia using awake navigation for verification. Post-operatively, patients received 50mg of dexamethasone intravenously every six hours for two days, followed by a tapering dose over the subsequent week. The primary outcome measured was the complete ablation rate, while secondary outcomes included complete or near-complete symptom improvement, neurological deficits, and surgical complications. Complete ablation was confirmed via T1-weighted contrast-enhanced MRI scans at one, three, and six months after the procedure. Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS version 24.0. The cohort consisted of 20 patients with an average age of 60.6±9.5 years, including 13 females. Complete ablation rates were 70% at one month, 80% at three months, and 90% at six months post-LITT. Complete symptom improvement was observed in 50% of patients, with 30% experiencing near-complete relief. No neurological deficits or surgical complications were recorded. Multivariate analysis identified the meningioma's maximum diameter as a significant predictor of complete ablation (p=0.018). These findings indicate that LITT is a safe, effective, and minimally invasive treatment for intracranial meningiomas, particularly suitable for high-risk patients who are not candidates for surgical resection or radiation therapy. Although large language models (LLMs) achieve human-level performance across many natural language tasks, their ability to handle knowledge-related duties—such as question answering and textual inference—remains limited when relying solely on textual data. This work investigates the potential of integrating knowledge graph (KG) structures into LLMs to enhance their capabilities with structured knowledge. We introduce StructuLLM, a framework where a knowledge graph is embedded within a base LLM (BaLLM) to create an infused model (IFLLM). Our approach involves encoding a structured KG into a one-hot vector and injecting this vector into the IFLLM's language model parameters. Extensive experiments using the StructuredQA dataset demonstrate that IFLLMs achieve significantly higher accuracy than both BaLLMs and standard LLMs on textual reasoning tasks. Furthermore, results indicate that IFLLMs generalize effectively to unseen knowledge graphs. These findings suggest that structured knowledge from knowledge graphs complements natural language sentences within large language models, yielding superior performance. Code is accessible at https://github.com/yangshengyu/StructuLLM.

This study investigates the connection between the shadow radius and temperature within a Born-Infeld AdS black hole framework under varying chemical potential conditions. The analysis reveals that, for a fixed spin parameter, the shadow radius exhibits non-monotonic behavior as temperature changes. Furthermore, the system's phase transition is characterized using a Van der Waals-like model, identifying a first-order transition linked to changes in the shadow radius alongside a Hawking-Page transition. A shadow-Temperature (R-T) plane is constructed to distinguish coexistence regions from gas-liquid and liquid-black hole phases. Additionally, a three-dimensional graph is employed to clarify the R-T dependencies across different chemical potentials and spin values. Finally, a thermal entropy-Sd plane is utilized to further examine the transition's nature; this examination confirms that the phase transition in the Born-Infeld AdS black hole under these specific conditions aligns with the observed variations in the black hole shadow. The findings suggest that the shadow radius serves as an effective probe for uncovering thermodynamic phase transitions. Regarding the broader context of high-energy physics, recent astrophysical observations of the cosmic microwave background indicate that the universe's expansion is accelerating, a phenomenon commonly attributed to dark energy. Concurrently, the image of a black hole shadow captured by the Event Horizon Telescope has spurred significant interest in exploring how dark energy, dark matter, and other high-energy physics concepts interact. In this context, recent research has focused on analyzing the shadow radius within dark energy contexts, while the current work extends this inquiry to the Born-Infeld AdS black hole framework. Recent theoretical investigations by some of the same authors have explored the shadow radius in connection with dark energy under similar conditions [30, 31]. From a mathematical physics perspective, the study of phase transitions remains a significant area of inquiry, with recent works examining these transitions in various physical contexts, including studies on superconductors [32], vacuum fluids [33], and even the concept of time [34]. Regarding the specific context of black holes, earlier research has explored phase transitions from multiple angles; for instance, Ref. [35] analyzed them in terms of the "order parameter," while Ref. [36] investigated them via the "response function." Ref. [37] specifically examined first-order phase transitions in charged anti-de Sitter (AdS) black holes through a temperature-Carnot efficiency plane, whereas Ref. [38] focused on non-extensive AdS black holes using a temperature-entropy plane.

While optical tomography has become a standard measurement technique in experiments with superconducting circuits, its application to the quantum state of light relies on integrating the optical tomogram with a yet-to-be-determined extraction method for the Wigner function. This work proposes a novel approach to derive the Q function directly from the optical tomogram, utilizing the Fourier transform, sliding transform, or their combination. The proposed method is validated through coherent, thermal, and squeezed states. Furthermore, the algorithm's capability to extract the Wigner function from the optical tomogram is demonstrated via interference between the quantum and classical components of a hybrid state of light. To achieve this, the team employed a beam splitter to create an optical equivalent of the Hadamard gate, and a electro-optic modulator (EOM) to act as a quantum gate generating a $|0\rangle\to|1\rangle$ flip contingent on the spin state (see Fig. 1). As a result, the quantum superposition in the light path arises from the spin-dependent beam deflection by the EOM, while the Wigner function of the light field is extracted from the optical tomogram using the proposed algorithm. Consequently, the interference between the quantum and classical aspects of the light's state is observed in the resulting reconstructed Q function (in the heat map of the Q representation) and its corresponding Wigner function (see Fig. 2). Ultimately, this study demonstrates that the Q function can be derived from the optical tomogram through the Fourier transform, sliding transform, or a combination of both; subsequently, the Wellendorf relation is employed to extract the Wigner function from the Q function, ultimately generating the optical analog of the Hadamard-test circuit. This study reports the initial observation of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay and provides evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode. The analysis utilizes a data set with an integrated luminosity of 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ from $pp$ collisions recorded by LHCb at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV. The measured branching fractions are given by:
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0) &=
(3.3\pm0.4\pm0.3(\text{unc})\pm0.2(\text{norm}))\times10^{-4}, \\
\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0) &=
(2.1\pm0.4\pm0.2(\text{unc})\pm0.1(\text{norm}))\times10^{-4},
\end{align*}
where the uncertainties listed are statistical, followed by systematic errors attributed to the charm branching fraction and other sources, and finally the error related to the normalization channel. Additionally, the ratio of the branching fractions for the two decay modes is determined to be $R_{\mathcal{B}}=0.64\pm0.14(\text{stat})\pm0.08(\text{syst})\pm0.05(\text{norm})$. It is further noted that the observed significance of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ mode is contingent upon the assumed value of the branching fraction for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay. The findings presented here are contingent upon the baryon branching fraction measurement from ATLAS. Future investigations will leverage the larger data sets anticipated from Run 2 at the LHC.

Generally, constructing the submodule lattice $L(M)$ for a specific module $M$ presents significant challenges. For certain classes of modules, explicit constructions of $L(M)$ are achievable through join irreducible submodules or by establishing an isomorphism with a known lattice. This paper introduces a construction method for $L(M)$ based on both maximal and join irreducible submodules. Applying this approach, we determine the submodule lattice for a broad class of modules defined by a set of monomial relations over a vector space, ultimately proving that this specific lattice is a geometric lattice. Additionally, we demonstrate that the resulting construction is not necessarily unique. Ultimately, we provide a circuit-based algorithm capable of computing the image of any element within $L(M)$. In terms of computational complexity, we establish that determining the image of a specified composition of a subset of monomial relation vectors to form a submodule is P-complete, whereas constructing $L(M)$ itself is #P-complete. Our entire construction process is implemented in Sage (https://sage.math.sourceforge.net). Furthermore, we outline potential applications of this method to other modules where a similar construction remains unexplored. Notably, we examine the monomial modules $M(\Gamma, f)$ associated with graphs $\Gamma$ and functions $f: V(\Gamma) \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$, confirming the feasibility of this construction in those contexts. Finally, we apply the method to $M(\Delta, \chi_{e})$, where $\Delta = K_{3,3}$ is the complete tripartite graph and $\chi_{e}$ corresponds to the edges of $\Delta$, revealing a previously unknown isomorphism between this lattice and the noncrossing partition lattice of $K_{3,3}$. We also confirm an isomorphism between $L(M(\Delta, \chi_{e}))$ and the sublattice of $NC(\Delta)$ comprising noncrossing partitions of $\Delta$ with at most $|e|$ edges. The proof of this final isomorphism requires an explicit, detailed construction of $L(M(\Gamma, f))$ involving numerous submodules, which might be difficult to achieve without the algorithm proposed in this work.

This study demonstrates that certain well-established recurrent operators—specifically the recurrent curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators—play a crucial role in determining whether biharmonic hypersurfaces are minimal within Euclidean space. Additionally, the paper introduces a new recurrence condition on the curvature operator and examines its implications forbiharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean environments. The analysis also covers recent findings related to recurrent curvature operators and their connection to biharmonic varieties. Finally, future directions for investigating the recurrence of the curvature operator and its influence onbiharmonic varieties are outlined. For any rational number $p/q$, numeration in base $p/q$ is defined by a function mapping finite words over the alphabet $\{0,1,...,p-1\}$ to rational values. The subset of words evaluating to nonnegative integers in base $p/q$ constitutes a classic example of a $p/q$-recognizable language, also known as a regular subset of $(p/q)^*$. This paper investigates the regularity of two related subsets: the set of words assessing to irreducible fractions and those assessing to zero. While the subsets of words evaluating to nonnegative integers and irreducible fractions form a hierarchy based on $(p/q)^*$, the set of words assessing to zero does not necessarily belong to this family. Specifically, we demonstrate that for $p/q=3/2$, the zero-set exhibits regularity, yet for $p/q=5/3$, it does not. Ultimately, we establish that the zero-set is regular if and only if $p$ is a multiple of $q(q-1)$. Furthermore, we define the set of integers (potentially negative) that are $n$-th powers in the $(p/q)$-base and prove its regularity. As an application, we examine the "baby Euclidean algorithm," which determines the $(p/q)$-base expansion of a rational; we provide an explicit formula for the set of $n$-th power integers where the Euclidean algorithm requires at most $k$ steps to find the leading digit, proving this set is finite and providing its canonical regular expression. Finally, we define a function counting the occurrences of $n$-th powers in the $(p/q)$-base of nonnegative integers within a range of size $N$, showing the explicit dependence on $N$ constitutes a polynomiairce.

This study conducts a comprehensive analysis of the chaotic dynamics inherent in the Duffing-Gruytenster household attractor, which exhibits a correlation dimension of 1.04 $\pm$ 0.05. The system under examination is a modified arrangement of the conventional setup, where the primary drive is replaced by a 90-degree phase-shifted secondary drive, and the damping coefficient is adjusted to yield an attractor with a correlation dimension close to unity. An extended state space is constructed using time-delay embedding, followed by the application of phase space stretching and folding techniques to determine the Lyapunov exponent. Subsequently, a reconstructed attractor is derived via the time-delay method, and its correlation dimension is evaluated using the Grassberger-Procaccia algorithm. Concurrently, the system's Lyapunov exponent and attractor are examined across a range of secondary drive amplitudes, while the correlation dimension is assessed at both low and high primary drive amplitude settings. Furthermore, the correlation dimension is calculated and compared under varying time delay conditions. Ultimately, a differentiable relationship between the secondary drive amplitude and the correlation dimension is established through a neural network model. The findings indicate that as the secondary drive amplitude increases, the attractor's shape becomes more complex, causing the correlation dimension to shift from a fractal value near 1.04 $\pm$ 0.05 to an integer value of 2, a phenomenon observed consistently at both low and high primary drive amplitudes. Additionally, the Lyapunov exponent demonstrates sensitivity to changes in the secondary drive amplitude, particularly within the range of 0.75 to 1.5, while the attractor's morphology evolves with variations in the time delay parameter.

In the early 1930s, K. Menger explored the concept of an abstract angle function, defining it broadly for metric and semi-metric spaces. He also formulated several properties that an angle function in a real vector space should satisfy to be considered reasonable. This paper aims to demonstrate that these properties are insufficient to guarantee that the angle function arises from a norm. Specifically, we provide a counterexample on $\R^2$ using a non-symmetric distance (a mere metric), which possesses a valid angle function satisfying all of Menger's conditions, yet which is not derivable from a norm. This counterexample implies that a triangle inequality involving four points and an angle function does not necessarily yield a fifth inequality among five points, highlighting a fundamental limitation of carathéodory-type principles when applied to mere metrics. To address this, we introduce a concept analogous to the Jordan-von Neumann derivation of a semi-inner product from a metric in a vector space, termed the "5-point metric derivation." We define this derivation for any mere metric space equipped with an angle function satisfying specific axioms and explicitly formulate the necessary and sufficient conditions for this derivation to constitute a semi-inner product. Finally, we show that this -point metric derivation aligns with the standard Glackmann-Rader definition when applied to genuine metrics on vector spaces. As an application of this framework, we offer a characterization of all spaces that admit a metric derivation. Additionally, we briefly discuss the feasibility of defining similar derivations in topological spaces. To support these ideas in such contexts, we generalize the notion of an angle function to a concept we call "angle preservation," and we introduce a definition of distance between subsets within a topological space.

Neural network-based point cloud models have achieved significant success and are extensively utilized in safety-critical domains, including Lidar recognition systems for autonomous vehicles. Nevertheless, these models remain susceptible to adversarial attacks designed to deceive predictions through stealthy semantic transformations like rotation and randomization. This paper introduces TPC, a transformation-specific smoothing framework that delivers tight and scalable robustness guarantees for point cloud models against such attacks. We begin by classifying common 3D transformations into three groups: additive (e.g., random noise), composable (e.g., rotation and randomization), and indirectly composable (e.g., shear). Specifically, we define a stealthy transformation function and a corresponding testing function to identify the most deceptive transformation within a defined space and strength. Furthermore, we directly optimize the guaranteed robustness against all transformations up to a specified strength within the defined space and stealthiness. Finally, we introduce a GRT-guaranteed smoothing method based on this TPC framework. Extensive experiments across diverse point cloud models and transformation spaces demonstrate that our approach is effective, where our guaranteed robustness is significantly higher than existing methods, and our testing speed is at least 1.92 times faster than state-of-the-art techniques. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/GarretYi/TPC. Neural models, Point clouds, Adversarial examples, Sematic transformations, Point cloud smoothing, and Robustness guarantees.

The verification techniques of formal methods have been underutilized in program testing and learning. This study introduces a novel approach to program testing integrated with the $\alpha$-theory of types, a term that is colloquially referred to as type checking. By employing a formal method for type checking, the research aims to automate program testing and facilitate the integration of verification into programming education. As a byproduct, this work also advances the testing of machine learning models. The core contribution of this paper is a unified framework for program testing that incorporates type checking, type inference, and type errors. This framework is constructed using the $\tau$-calculus, which extends the $\lambda$-calculus with the $\alpha$-theory of types. To enable automation within this framework, a learning-based algorithm for type checking is employed, specifically a neural network-guided approach known as VETTA. Furthermore, the framework leverages a learning-based algorithm for semantic typing called VETT to embed types into neural representations. To validate this framework, a language called $\tau$-Fun was developed and released as open source (https://github.com/hhhuang/tfetta), serving as the operational platform for automating program testing via the VETTA and VETT algorithms. To demonstrate the utility of this framework, a competitive machine learning model training was conducted to identify the most accurate algorithm for classifying terms in the $\tau$-calculus. Additionally, the framework was utilized to verify a prior finding from learning theory regarding the linearity of type classification in neural networks. Finally, the value of this verification framework for enhancing programming learning is explored, and a meta-learning model was developed to learn how to locate errors within this framework.

This paper presents an explicit formulation of the weight component of Serre's conjecture for GL_2, grounded in Kummer theory and deliberately avoiding p-adic Hodge theory. The approach relies on characterizing the reduction modulo p of crystalline extensions via specific "Kummer conditions." As a practical application, the explicit nature of this theory enables the development of an algorithm capable of computing the predicted local Langlands correspondence for any given prime p and a set of local conditions. Furthermore, when the weight is explicit and satisfies certain constraints, SageMath implementations of both this work and the known formulations are employed to verify the conjecture regarding the correspondence's explicit description. The implementation within this work proves particularly advantageous when the prime is not small and the diagonal entry of the local condition at 1 is substantial. Ultimately, the methods outlined here may facilitate future efforts to extend these techniques to higher-dimensional cases. Notably, [RW14] demonstrates that for GL_n, knowing the conjecture's statement for n=2 allows one to deduce it for any rank r≥2 when ladic representations are considered; however, an explicit version when working modulo p remains an open challenge. Fiber-reinforced composites featuring nanofiller-modified polymer matrices hold significant promise for enhancing the safety of high-risk engineering structures. These materials possess an inherent self-sensing capability, as their electrical conductivity alters in response to deformation and damage. This phenomenon, termed piezoresistivity, has been widely utilized for damage detection through electrical resistance measurements and tomographic imaging methods like electrical impedance tomography (EIT). However, existing approaches often struggle with accuracy when identifying larger damages via EIT. This study introduces a hybrid framework combining a deep learning algorithm and gauge theory to enhance damage detection using EIT data for a 3D embedded carbon nanofiber (CNF) reinforced polyurethane elastomer (PU) composite containing a sharp notch. The composite was subjected to mode-I fracture and mode-III torsion loading, with the resulting impedance data fed into the proposed deep learning model. The framework achieved high detection accuracy for various Mode-I and Mode-III damages under different loading conditions. Furthermore, the study examined the influence of CNF volume fractions and material anisotropy on the quality of the reconstructed conductivity images. Findings indicate that a CNF volume fraction of 0.25 % yielded the optimal image quality, while increasing anisotropy by rotating the fiber orientation relative to the loading direction degraded the reconstruction accuracy.

We introduce a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces that prioritizes geometric and algebraic foundations, utilizing the decomposition of tensors into scalar, vector, and higher-order components. This approach employs a distinct notation system and defines tensor components with respect to an orthonormal basis, which is further expressed through a chosen origin and unit vector components. The utility of this methodology is demonstrated by reformulating numerous standard identities and theorems from vector calculus and matrix theory using tensor notation. Additionally, the proposed formalism offers a straightforward means to establish isomorphisms between tensors in Euclidean spaces and those in Minkowski space. To facilitate this, we extend the concept of raising and lowering indices from Euclidean to Minkowski tensors, incorporating an analogous operation for Euclidean tensors. Ultimately, this work serves as a companion to our earlier study on an analogous formalism for Minkowski space \cite{arxiv1909.03600}. We demonstrate that if a right-angled Artin group $A(\Gamma)$ admits a non-trivial, minimal action on a tree $T$ that is not a line, then $\Gamma$ must contain a separating subgraph $\Lambda$ for which $A(\Lambda)$ stabilizes an edge in $T$. Leveraging this result, we provide explicit constructions of actions on $T$ that fail to be residually finite. As a specific application, we examine the group $A(\Gamma_{3,2})$, where $\Gamma_{3,2}$ represents the "3-2" graph (a triangle with two additional vertices connected to a single vertex of valency one). Utilizing distinct actions on $T$, we compose maps along a product of trees $T \times T \times T$ to define two actions $\rho_1$ and $\rho_2$ on $A(\Gamma_{3,2})$ that are equivariant with respect to the product tree structure. However, we prove that no group homomorphism $f : A(\Gamma_{3,2}) \to G$ can exist that simultaneously satisfies $f(\rho_1(w)) = \rho_1'(w)$ and $f(\rho_2(w)) = \rho_2'(w)$ for every word $w$ in the generators of $A(\Gamma_{3,2})$, where $\rho_1'$ and $\rho_2'$ denote any actions on another tree $T'$. Finally, as a direct consequence, we establish that the derived action $\bar{\rho}_3$ on the quotient of $A(\Gamma_{3,2})$ by the normal closure of the relation $y_1 y_2 y_3 y_2 y_1 y_3 y_2 y_1 = 1$ remains undefined on at least one element of $A(\Gamma_{3,2})$. To achieve this, we explicitly identify a relation $r$ equivalent to the specified word that is also expressible as a product of commutators involving elements of $A(\Lambda)$, where $\Lambda$ is either $\Gamma_{3,2}$ itself or a subgraph of $\Gamma_{3,2}$.

Advancements in technology have enabled the collection of massive datasets, while increased computational power has allowed for the development of direct matrix inversion methods capable of handling high-dimensional data. Nevertheless, iterative approaches remain a viable option for processing large datasets. These methods offer benefits such as reduced memory requirements and the ability to invert matrices that are otherwise too large for direct techniques, including sparse and structured matrices. Furthermore, iterative algorithms can be executed on graphics processing units (GPUs) and implemented in real-time. This paper evaluates nine iterative matrix inversion methods, comparing them against a classic direct method using four distinct large-scale datasets. The assessment covers convergence rates, linear convergence factors, and other relevant metrics. The results indicate that the Chebyshev, Hermitian Chebyshev, Newton, and rational Newton iterations performed comparably across the tested datasets. Additionally, an anticipated linear convergence factor was found to be a reliable indicator of the per-step speed of these iterative methods. To facilitate future research, the four datasets utilized in this study are made accessible via Google Drive at the following link: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/11900360633f9e2037f873887e575223. This study addresses the performance limits of contextual linear bandits (LIBits), a model where agents learn optimal decisions through experience in time-varying environments, with contexts encoded using $d$ bits per dimension and histories constrained by $B$ total bits per context. While prior research has primarily focused on fully observable LIBits—yielding a lower bound of $d+B$ bits per context and an upper bound involving $\sqrt{d}+B$—this work investigates a distributed memoryless LIBits framework. In this setup, contexts are approximately $d$-dimensional vectors accessible only to a local learner, whereas actions and rewards are observable by all participants. Leveraging this model, we establish both an upper bound on regret (the loss relative to the optimal linear strategy) and a corresponding lower bound. Specifically, we propose an algorithm achieving a regret upper bound of $O(d + \sqrt{d}B + N)$, where $N$ represents bits per dimension for the distributed contexts. Furthermore, utilizing approximately $5d$ bits per context and $\log_2 B$ bits per context dimension, we derive a lower bound of $\Omega(d + \sqrt{d}B)$, which matches the proposed algorithm's bound when contexts are approximately five dimensions. These findings highlight that, for large contexts, a linear number of bits per context is necessary, whereas the bits required per context dimension can decrease. To validate these theoretical outcomes, we also present experimental results from a geographic routing task.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism influenced by dust in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. While the VSI generates gas turbulence and rapid dust settling, conventional models assume dust grains remain constant in size. This study examines how dust growth interacts with VSI-driven turbulence. We employ the fast radial-infall model of dust settling, coupled with a top-down growth model where outer-region dust collides and aggregates into larger clumps. Utilizing a 2D version of the global FUC-FOUR code, we run N-body simulations tracking individual dust particles alongside hydrodynamical gas simulations. Our results indicate that dust growth amplifies VSI activity in the outer disk: settling enhances local gas density (exceeding 10$^{-3}$ cm$^{-3}$), while reduced thermal conduction in this dense layer fosters instability. Furthermore, the transition from numerous small to fewer large particles increases settling velocity and local density. In our most extreme simulation, dust settles from a 20 au initial scale height down to 0.5 au within 10,000 years, with growth accelerating as particles enlarge. This rapid settling and growth effectively decouples outer-region dust from inner-region gas dynamics, potentially explaining the clear annular structures observed in dust emission by ALMA. Consequently, top-down growth models combined with VSI turbulence should be considered when analyzing dust structures in the outer zones of protonecteen-type protoplanetary disks. These models can also account for the separation between gas and dust dynamics seen in Herbig Be disk outer regions, where binary stellar interactions drive tidal instabilities. Ultimately, understanding dust growth and its coupling with turbulence is essential for reconstructing the timescales and physical processes in protoplanetary disks. These insights are crucial for identifying where planet-forming conditions exist within these disks.

This study examines harmonic functions defined on gradient shrinking Ricci solitons that possess constant scalar curvature. We establish a Liouville theorem without relying on gradient estimates, demonstrating that any bounded harmonic function must be constant on such solitons. As a consequence, we prove that the dimension of the space of harmonic functions exhibiting polynomial growth is finite. Additionally, we derive a strong Liouville result confirming that all harmonic functions are constant. As an application, we provide a novel proof that the Gaussian soliton is the only soliton with constant scalar curvature in two dimensions. Finally, we discuss the potential implications of this work for future research.

The rise of machine learning has introduced novel vulnerabilities, including backdoor attacks, which remain a significant concern in security research. These attacks operate by embedding a trapdoor into the model during training; once deployed, the model executes a malicious function whenever it encounters a specific trigger hidden within the input. While prior studies have primarily concentrated on image classification systems, this work investigates backdoor mechanisms across various tasks and architectures. We introduce a new attack method for neural networks called "Cosmic," which remains undetectable even when models are subjected to extensive logging and adversarial testing. Cosmic integrates seamlessly with existing backdoor protocols, utilizing an obfuscated trigger that conceals its presence within input images through subtle color shifts imperceptible to humans. Furthermore, we extend this concept to video data, developing a variant named "Cosmic-Video," which employs a frame-based trigger to activate the trapdoor. This report outlines the approaches that secured second and third place in task 2 of the ISIC 2019 challenge, which aims to support skin cancer diagnosis using dermoscopic images. The goal is to identify five specific diagnoses from a set of potential skin lesions: melanoma, melanocytoma, basal cell carcinoma, seborrheic keratosis, and actinic keratosis. The proposed method involves a two-stage process: a support vector machine (SVM) is initially employed to distinguish between melanoma and the other four conditions, and a convolutional neural network (CNN) classifier is then applied to differentiate the remaining lesion types. Additionally, an ensemble of three classifiers was developed to rank the probable diagnoses for melanocytic lesions, with this voting mechanism integrated into the final system. This study examines the coherence of electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino behavior, and dark matter properties within the minimal scoto-seesaw framework, extending the simplest implementation by introducing one complex scalar triplet and two singlet scalars. The analysis covers a broad range of parameters, covering both low- and high-scale dynamics. It is demonstrated that satisfying limits on neutrino oscillation lengths requires the distinction between the 'atmospheric' and 'solar' mass scales to be substantial, implying that weak-scale dynamics occur at the 'atmospheric' scale while dark sector dynamics unfold at the 'solar' scale. Furthermore, a model point achieving the correct thermal abundance of dark matter is found only when the 'solar' scale resides in the TeV range. Focusing on this 'TeV-seesaw' configuration, the study comprehensively maps out the validity of effective field theory, identifies new physics resonances, and determines the outcomes of parton collider experiments across various energies. Additionally, the work explores implications for future fixed-target and beam-dump facilities. Finally, the model is assessed against existing data, including direct searches for dark matter, neutron-electric dipole moment constraints, and anomalies from $B\to K(\nu\nu)\mu^+\mu^-$ and meson mixing. Overall, the 'TeV-seesaw' represents a viable framework capable of addressing mass hierarchies, explaining dark matter, and justifying the weakness of the dark force, with future experiments poised to test multiple of its predictions. Notably, this validity holds even when co-annealing dark matter with heavy 2-singlet scalars. To support future investigations into the dark sector, a public implementation of the model in FeynArts/FormCalc is available at https://github.com/gbrooke/scoto-seesaw.
